entries.name: pair-items-mismatch-false#0
entries.script: { If(false, Coll[(Int, Int)](), Coll[(Long, Long)]()) == Coll[(Int, Int)]() }  // JVM: false. equalDataValues charges MatchType and then returns false on an item-type difference, before comparing any item (DataValueComparer.scala:323). Both sides are EMPTY, so an implementation that compares items one by one finds nothing to disagree about and answers true — PAIR items are one of the composite kinds sigma-rust does not item-type-check. Value.checkType cannot stop the tree getting here: isValueOfType asks only isInstanceOf[Coll[_]] for a collection (SType.scala:198), so the declared Coll[Int] is satisfied by a Coll[Long]

entries.name: nested-coll-mismatch-false#1
entries.script: { If(false, Coll[Coll[Int]](), Coll[Coll[Long]]()) == Coll[Coll[Int]]() }  // JVM: false. equalDataValues charges MatchType and then returns false on an item-type difference, before comparing any item (DataValueComparer.scala:323). The NESTED-collection twin of #0, the other composite kind that goes item-by-item in sigma-rust. Value.checkType cannot stop the tree getting here: isValueOfType asks only isInstanceOf[Coll[_]] for a collection (SType.scala:198), so the declared Coll[Int] is satisfied by a Coll[Long]

entries.name: primitive-items-mismatch-false#2
entries.script: { If(false, Coll[Int](), Coll[Long]()) == Coll[Int]() }  // JVM: false. The PRIMITIVE-item control: equalDataValues charges MatchType and then returns false on an item-type difference, before comparing any item (DataValueComparer.scala:323), and sigma-rust does check item types for primitives, so this row is false on both and is what rules the If shape out as the cause of #0 and #1

entries.name: same-item-types-true#3
entries.script: { Coll[(Int, Int)]() == Coll[(Int, Int)]() }  // JVM: true. The same-item-type control — two empty pair collections ARE equal, so #0's false is the item-type difference and not emptiness. NOTE this tree has no If, so its cost is not the counterpart of #0's; #7 is

entries.name: filter-keeps-input-item-type-false#4
entries.script: { If(false, Coll[Int](1), Coll[Long](2L)).filter({ (x: Long) => false }) == Coll[Int]() }  // JVM: false. Coll.filter keeps the INPUT's item type, so filtering a Coll[Long] down to nothing yields an empty Coll[LONG], which is unequal to an empty Coll[Int]. equalDataValues charges MatchType and then returns false on an item-type difference, before comparing any item (DataValueComparer.scala:323). This is the row that needs the element-type gate gone first — see Coll.hof_element_type_mismatch — so an implementation still gating Filter rejects here instead of answering false

entries.name: pair-items-mismatch-neq-true#5
entries.script: { If(false, Coll[(Int, Int)](), Coll[(Long, Long)]()) != Coll[(Int, Int)]() }  // JVM: true — #0 under NEQ. equalDataValues charges MatchType and then returns false on an item-type difference, before comparing any item (DataValueComparer.scala:323), and NEQ negates it

entries.name: nested-coll-mismatch-neq-true#6
entries.script: { If(false, Coll[Coll[Int]](), Coll[Coll[Long]]()) != Coll[Coll[Int]]() }  // JVM: true — #1 under NEQ. equalDataValues charges MatchType and then returns false on an item-type difference, before comparing any item (DataValueComparer.scala:323), and NEQ negates it

entries.name: same-shape-honest-true#7
entries.script: { If(false, Coll[(Int, Int)](), Coll[(Int, Int)]()) == Coll[(Int, Int)]() }  // JVM: true. The SAME-SHAPE honest twin of #0 — identical tree but for the false branch's item types, so the cost difference against #0 is the item-type mismatch alone and nothing else. This is the row to read #0's cost against, not #3
